title: Backpressure signal fidelity bench - proxy & client pathways
content:
Purpose:
This is an exploratory bench to measure how faithfully backpressure signals propagate across different client/proxy/server stacks. We've seen flakiness in tail latency correlated with client flush timing + proxy buffering; hypothesis is that some proxy paths mask or distort TCP/TLS-level signals which leads to ineffective KV cache warmup and microburst amplification.

Scope / what we measured:
- Protocols: HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 (gRPC streaming), gRPC-web (browser-like path)
- Proxies: edge-proxy-v1 (current prod), edge-proxy-v2 (new pacing), nginx-1.26 (baseline), envoy-1.30 (with dynamic watermarks)
- Clients: Go net/http client (single connection), Python aiohttp (concurrent coroutines), node-fetch (emulated browser), synthetic microbench client that intentionally delays first flush
- Server: serving-runtime-local-x86 (single model instance), kv-cache enabled/disabled
- Workloads: short-answer chat (prompt 20 tokens, response 80–200), long generative (prompt 50, response 800–1200)
- Metrics collected: per-request tail p50/p95/p99 latency, first-byte latency (time-to-first-token), bytes-in-flight over time, TCP cwnd traces (where available), TLS record sizes, application-level ACKs/flow-control frames (HTTP/2), KV cache hit ratio.

Experimental matrix (high level):
- Crossed protocol X proxy X client X workload X kv-cache setting = ~144 runs; each run = 10k requests (steady-state after 1k warmup)
- Synthetic injected microbursts: 10–100 concurrent ephemeral requests to create queueing pressure
- Backpressure manipulations: client-side flush hold (0ms, 10ms, 50ms, 200ms), proxy buffer window (default, low-watermark 32KB, high-watermark 512KB)

Key implementation notes / instrumentation hacks:
- Instrumented proxy with lightweight tracing to emit flush events (proxy emits PROXY_FLUSH event in trace log) and buffer occupancy every 5ms (added to v2 branch).
- Kernel TCP cwnd sampled with eBPF probe on loadgen machines (coarse, but useful for trends).
- Added a tiny patch to runtime to emit "kv-warmup-observed:true/false" for each request (non-invasive, sampled 1%).
- Where TLS record sizes are not accessible (closed-source managed proxies), we infer from observed chunk sizes at application layer.

High-level results (summary):
- When client holds first flush >50ms, kv-cache warmup drops by 28–45% for short-answer workload on edge-proxy-v1; effect amplified when proxy buffer high-watermark is large (>=256KB).
- Envoy with dynamic watermarks preserved signal fidelity best: first-byte latency increased slightly (~2–6ms) but tail p99 decreased by up to 18ms versus nginx baseline in microburst scenarios.
- gRPC streaming (HTTP/2) preserved application-level flow-control signals more reliably than HTTP/1.1 chunked over nginx, especially for small token bursts. Observed 12% lower p95 on average for short-answer workload.
- gRPC-web path (via envoy + translation) introduced a path where client flushes were coalesced into fixed-size frames, leading to >30% mismatch between application flush intent and actual egress timing — this caused kv-cache warmup to be ineffective.
- TLS record coalescing by some proxies masked microflushes: when TLS coalescing was enabled in the proxy, effective token inter-arrival at server looked bursty (larger records at slower cadence).

Representative numbers (short-answer workload, kv-cache enabled):
- edge-proxy-v1 + Go client + default proxy buffers: p50=18ms, p95=73ms, p99=190ms, first-byte=12ms, kv-warmup-hit=62%
- nginx + Python client + flush 50ms: p50=22ms, p95=86ms, p99=260ms, first-byte=18ms, kv-warmup-hit=44%
- envoy-dynamic + Go client + flush 0ms: p50=20ms, p95=65ms, p99=172ms, first-byte=14ms, kv-warmup-hit=71%
(see full CSV artifacts linked in tickets)

Observations / interpretation:
- Signal fidelity is a property of the entire path, not just server or client. Proxies that implement aggressive coalescing or that buffer to high-water marks tend to blunt the fine-grained inter-token timing that helps kv-cache warm paths.
- HTTP/2's flow-control frames provide a richer signal surface; when proxies preserve these frames end-to-end (Envoy did in our setup) the server can start streaming earlier and warm KV cache more effectively.
- Small delays at the client (10–50ms) are catastrophic for short bursts in presence of proxy buffering because they shift arrival patterns into larger lumps that trigger scheduling backpressure in the runtime.
- There is a tradeoff: disabling TLS coalescing or lowering proxy buffer sizes improves fidelity but increases connection churn/packet rate and CPU overhead on proxies. Need cost model.

Anomalies / gotchas we hit:
- Some managed edge proxies we used in the 3rd-party test had closed-source internals that rewrite TLS records (coalescing). We had to infer behavior; results should be considered with caution.
- eBPF cwnd sampling showed high variance under microbursts (probing interference). Use as qualitative only.
- A regression in our patch caused kv-warmup flag to be dropped at 0.1% sampling; fixed in PR 462.

Immediate action items / next steps:
- (A) Shepherd minimal envoy config that preserves HTTP/2 flow-control frames and disables TLS coalescing for a canary path. Owner: Grace Park. JIRA: INF-1337. Target: 2 weeks.
- (B) Add per-route proxy buffer config to Dedicated beta so customers can opt into lower buffer windows for latency-sensitive routes. Owner: Luis Martinez. Add to backlog.
- (C) Run cost model: estimate CPU/egress tradeoffs when disabling coalescing vs observed tail latency improvements (SRE + infra). Owner: Tom Nguyen.
- (D) Instrument client SDKs (Go/Node/Python) to expose an opt-in "flush-intent" header so proxies can be explicitly configured to avoid coalescing those flows. Prototype (RFC) in GH branch.

Notes to self / open questions:
- Does our upstream load-balancer (LB) re-chunk or re-buffer at TLS layer? Need to capture a packet-level pcap near LB and proxy side-by-side.
- Should we add a small 1–2ms jitter to client flushes to avoid pathological alignment that causes bursts? Could be cheaper than changing proxy config. Risk: increased p50.
- How do mobile SDKs behave (iOS/Android)? They often use platform HTTP stacks that may batch writes; need a mobile-run.

- JIRA: INF-1337 (envoy dynamic watermark config + canary)
- PR: serving-runtime/pull/462 (kv-warmup sampling fix)

Closing thought:
We should aim for a short-term mitigation (envoy per-route buffer tuning + client opt-in header) and a medium-term product story: "latency-sensitive routes" profile in Console that sets buffer/watermark/pacing defaults optimized for kv-cache warmup and streaming fidelity.
